text: Thérèse Schwartze got her first training from her father, the painter Johan Georg Schwartze. She studied for a year at the Rijksacademie and then went to Munich to work under Gabriel Max and Franz von Lenbach. In 1879 she went to Paris to study with Jean-Jacques Henner. Back in Amsterdam she joined Arti et Amicitiae, and she showed her work at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago. Most of her sitters came from the city's elite. She married Anton van Duyl late in life and then added his name to her signature.

Eduard Veith first trained to follow his father, a decorative painter. He went on to Vienna to study at the Museum of Applied Arts under Ferdinand Laufberger, and he made sgraffito for exhibition buildings at the Paris Exposition Universelle. Back home he helped his father paint churches and synagogues. After study trips to Italy, Belgium and Tunisia he settled in Vienna as a freelance artist. Franz Joseph I ordered the big ceiling fresco he painted in the Maria-Theresia-Saal of the Hofburg. He died in Vienna in 1925.

Adolphe Willette studied for four years at the École des Beaux-Arts under Alexandre Cabanel. He made Pierrot an imaginary hero of France and gave Mimi Pinson her frail, lovable, good-hearted character. His work ranged from dainty trifles to political satire, and the guillotine and Death appear in his caricatures. He sent many drawings to the French illustrated press, some under pen names such as Cémoi and Pierrot. He also painted walls, stained glass and a ceiling for cabarets and music halls, among them Le Chat noir and La Cigale. During the Dreyfus affair he sided against Dreyfus and moved to the political right with Jean-Louis Forain.

Jan Davidsz. de Heem studied first under his father, a painter, and then under Balthasar van der Ast. He spent a few years in Leiden, where he also took lessons from David Bailly. After that he moved to the Southern Netherlands and joined the Guild of Saint Luke in Antwerp in 1635 or 1636. He was so much in demand that he could hardly meet the orders. A portrait of Prince William III in a frame of flowers and fruit sold for 2000 guilders. He died in Antwerp before the end of April 1684.

Elin Danielson's father went bankrupt when the family farm failed in the Finnish famine, and her mother took on many jobs to pay for her daughters' schooling. At 15 she moved to Helsinki to study at the Academy of Fine Arts. Later she took lessons at the Académie Colarossi in Paris. A scholarship took her to Florence, and a year later she moved to the village of Antignano, where she met the painter Raffaello Gambogi, who was 13 years younger. They began working together. They married in 1898, and she died in Antignano in 1919, mostly forgotten in Finland.

By the age of 15 El Lissitzky was already teaching students of his own. The St. Petersburg Academy of Arts turned him down, so he went to Germany in 1909 to study architectural engineering at the Darmstadt Polytechnic Institute. He worked as a bricklayer on the side, and on vacations he drew the interior of the medieval Worms Synagogue. He began his career illustrating Yiddish children's books, and later he worked with Kazimir Malevich on suprematism and developed his own Proun series. In 1921 he moved to the Weimar Republic. He brought big changes to typography, exhibition design and book design.

Simeon Solomon got his first painting lessons from his older brother Abraham around 1850. As a student at the Royal Academy Schools he met Dante Gabriel Rossetti, the poet Swinburne and Edward Burne-Jones. His first show at the Academy came in 1858. He painted scenes from the Hebrew Bible and genre pictures of Jewish life and rituals, along with the literary subjects the Pre-Raphaelites liked. A public scandal after his arrest in 1873 cut his career short. Oscar Wilde and Walter Pater collected his work.
